# Introduction

An experimental study, in cognitive science as in other disciplines, passes through many hands and computerized systems. It is designed, evaluated, approved, preregistered, run, analyzed, reported, reviewed as a manuscript, used as training data, and rebuilt by a replicator. Each stage typically creates its own artifacts (e.g., data, diagrams, text files, code). Critically, there are no robust mechanisms to ensure that those artifacts remain consistent. Because each artifact carries its own copy of the study's parameters (with different copies typically containing overlapping subsets of information), there is a substantial risk that copies drift apart and information about the study becomes ambiguous, inaccurate, or plainly wrong. Such drift has been documented at several stages of a study's lifecycle, from design through reporting. For instance, only nine of 67 audited studies reported their outcomes faithfully [@goldacre2019compare], and only 11 of 35 open-data articles could be reproduced without author assistance [@hardwicke2018cognition, see Appendix 1 for a review].

One key reason for these consistency failures is the lack of standardized processes. Over the past decade, there have been notable efforts toward standardizing data, i.e., how data are formatted, organized in files, named, and shared [see, e.g., @bids; @nwb2023; @psychds; @bdm], an objective that undoubtedly remains essential. However, standardized data alone are insufficient to close the reproducibility gap. We also need *standardized processes* that cover the entire research pipeline [@aguilar2022experiments; @momeni2026guidelines].

Processes are harder to standardize than data because experimental studies can be complex, involve many actors, stakeholders, and tools, and serve a variety of purposes. These processes are currently handled in idiosyncratic, fragmented ways. They may be described in prose or hand-made diagrams and scattered across project documents, lab handbooks, slides, or custom code [@osc2015; @nosek2022replicability]. Despite initiatives to promote greater standardization of processes (typically through voluntary narrative reporting, preregistration, or data sharing), adoption of these practices remains limited [@hardwicke2024prevalence]. Furthermore, when standards are based only on narrative reporting, checking a study against them requires substantial human effort and is subjective and error-prone.

Finally, current practices are not flexible enough to handle the dynamic nature of studies. A preregistration, for example, fixes a static plan before a study starts but cannot always track the gap between that plan and what actually happened during its execution [@claesen2021adherence; @hardwicke2023preregistration]. The Methods section of a publication does not fully record what happened either [@carp2012secret; @errington2021challenges].

The problem with current practices is partly motivational, since the added effort of adopting and applying those practices may not yield immediate benefits. However, simply convincing more people to endorse current standards will not suffice. The root problem is structural, and addressing it requires standardizing research *processes*.

This structural problem lies in how research processes are currently written down, in prose and in custom code. There are fundamental reasons why this combination cannot keep a study's artifacts consistent. A software program does two things [@gelernter1992coordination]. It computes (shows a stimulus, scores a response, fits a model), and it coordinates those computations into a whole (their order, the conditions that decide which one runs next, and the data each provides or consumes). Experimental studies may share the code that computes but typically leave the coordination implicit, spread across function calls and shared variables. This implicit coordination is exactly where information drift accumulates. A workflow notation makes the coordination explicit, in a form people can easily understand and verify. Moreover, both prose and code have key limitations. Prose is accessible to most humans but is subject to interpretation. For example, the same question given to many analysts returns many distinct analyses [@silberzahn2018manyanalysts; @botviniknezer2020variability], and a language model can read the same protocol differently from one context to the next [@sclar2024prompt]. Code, on the other hand, is unambiguous but substantially limits the number of people who can understand the study. Fortunately, this is a common problem with a known solution, namely a coordination language that is both readable and unambiguous.

The solution we propose to overcome the challenges listed above rests on several key insights. There must be a single artifact that holds both the process and the data models, and is used across every stage of the research by all the stakeholders involved. Reproducibility must be a core property of that self-contained artifact, rather than optional documentation that lives beside it. Addressing the various use cases described above led us to a small set of design principles for such an artifact (@reltbl-principles). Appendix 1 reviews current approaches, including workflow engines, experiment builders, reporting guidelines, data standards, and visual notations. Studyflow, the solution we present here, is a visual notation that gives the experimental process a single representation that is machine-readable, human-understandable, and executable. One diagram serves at once as the protocol, the runnable study, the data model, the analysis specification, the provenance (i.e., the record of what was done), and the publication figure. Each of these is the same artifact seen by a different audience, rather than a distinct artifact (@fig-overview). In other words, Studyflow is a visual coordination language for experimental studies, written for both domain experts and technical experts. The computations stay in the tools built for them, while a Studyflow diagram carries the order of steps, the decisions, and the data dependencies that currently live in preregistrations, manuscripts, slides, data registries, and ad hoc scripts.

![**One diagram in place of many artifacts.** (A) Current practice, with many artifacts across the four stages of a study's lifecycle (Design, Run, Analyze, Report), information repeated across them, and each stakeholder using a different artifact. (B) Families of tools and the stages each covers. (C) The Studyflow approach, with an example study as one diagram that spans all four stages (shown in full in @fig-combined), and three of the views generated from it (Schedule, Provenance, Checklist).](figures/png/fig-overview.studyflow.png){#fig-overview}

The design of Studyflow follows from the realization that the problem at hand meets the classic criteria for preferring a domain-specific language [i.e., a notation built around one field's recurring structures, @mernik2005dsl] over general-purpose languages and tools (e.g., Python, workflow engines). However, rather than inventing a new language from scratch, Studyflow extends a tried-and-tested notation that many engineers and researchers already recognize, the Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN 2.0; @glosstbl-glossary defines this and the other technical terms used in the paper). BPMN is an expressive and well-documented standard for visually describing complex processes [@bpmnspec; @white2004introduction]. It is widely adopted [@geiger2016bpmn] and has been extended and applied in research and clinical settings [@braun2014; @dhond2021projectflow; @knight2024visualizing; @pufahl2022; @zarour2019].

This paper makes three key contributions. The first is the Studyflow *notation*, which is a domain-specific BPMN 2.0 profile (i.e., an extension that adds element types without changing the standard) that carries the elements experimental research needs. The notation is defined by a set of schemas and supported by open source tools released under the MIT license. It makes BPMN accessible to researchers who run experiments, in cognitive science and beyond, by presenting it in the language of experimental design. The second contribution of this work is a formal account of the Studyflow *diagram* that precisely defines what a diagram contains, when it is well-formed, how each view is derived from it, and how it runs (Materials and methods). Finally, the third contribution is a demonstration of Studyflow's capabilities. We test whether multiple undisclosed changes to a preregistered study are detected, and we run an example study end to end from one diagram. In that example study, cohorts of artificial participants follow the protocol of a CONSORT-style randomized trial. They are enrolled, screened, allocated to experimental groups, administered a Flanker and a Simon task in two separate sessions, excluded if they meet certain criteria, analyzed, and reported on, all through that single Studyflow diagram. We used artificial agents as participants in this demonstration for convenience; the same protocol could be administered to human cohorts through the same interface. Together, these contributions demonstrate that a single Studyflow diagram can support the complete study lifecycle in a way that is robust, efficient, reproducible, transparent, and auditable.
